## Jeremiah 33: verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the place should be translated "court of the guard" (see 32:2). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/33.htm
- Ellicott says this message comes from the same period as chapter 32 and has the same general character. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/33-1.htm
- Gill [Baptist; StudyLight calls him "Calvinist… Baptist"] says "second time" doesn't mean God had spoken to Jeremiah only twice. It means the second message on the same subject: the Messiah and the church's happiness. God's presence made the prison a palace, and though the prophet was bound, God's word was not. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-33.html
- Benson says that when Jeremiah was forced out of the temple, God followed him into prison. The people's persecution of the prophet could not cancel God's promises of mercy after the captivity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/jeremiah-33.html
- The Geneva notes [Reformed] place the court of the guard in the king's house in Jerusalem. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Jeremiah/33.html
- Precept Austin links this to Paul's words in 2 Timothy 2:9: Paul was in prison, but God's word is not. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_33_commentary

**v. 2**
- The Pulpit Commentary translates: "Jehovah, who doeth it, who frameth it that he may establish it." The unnamed "it" is God's great purpose of making his people new. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/33.htm
- Clarke reads "the doer of it": the God who will carry out what he is about to promise. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/33-2.html
- Benson says many interpreters take "it" to mean Jerusalem, a picture of the church. He also gives Blaney's version, where "it" is the thing God is about to do. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/jeremiah-33.html
- Geneva also takes "it" as Jerusalem: the God who made the city will keep it safe. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Jeremiah/33.html
- Matthew Henry says the maker of heaven and earth has all power. He ties this back to Jeremiah's prayer in 32:17. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_033.cfm
- The Spanish edition of Enduring Word stresses the name Yahweh, the name tied to God's covenant with Israel. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/jeremias-33/

**v. 3**
- Gill says the verse is spoken to the prophet, not the city, to encourage him to pray. The Hebrew can mean "fortified" things: things beyond human reason, which Gill calls "the great things of the Gospel." He says they can't mean the fall of Jerusalem, which Jeremiah already knew about. They are the spiritual blessings that follow. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/33-3.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-33.html
- Commentators disagree on the key word:
  - The Pulpit Commentary prefers "secret" (literally "inaccessible") things. It admits the rest of the chapter doesn't really contain any special secrets.
  - Ellicott prefers "mighty," because the same pair of words appears in Deuteronomy 1:28 and 9:1.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/33-3.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/33-1.htm
- Commentators also disagree on who is being invited to call:
  - Keil & Delitzsch argue it is not a personal word to Jeremiah. Nothing in the text says "to me." They read it as an appeal to the people to turn to the Lord in their disaster.
  - Benson and Gill take it as addressed to Jeremiah.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/33-3.htm
- Spurgeon [Baptist] finds three things here: a large promise, a hint that God's people don't yet know everything, and an application to "gospel doctrines." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/jeremiah-33.html
- Matthew Henry says comfort is obtained by prayer. Jeremiah had already prayed (32:16) but had to pray again. God gives promises to spur prayer, not to replace it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/33-2.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/33.htm
- Precept Austin quotes two preachers:
  - F. B. Meyer: little prayer brings little blessing, much prayer brings much blessing.
  - Adrian Rogers: this is a command to pray, not just an invitation.
  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_33_commentary
- The Pulpit Commentary (homiletics section) adds a caution. Praying did not get Jeremiah out of prison. God may choose to bless us in our troubles rather than remove them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-33.html

**vv. 4–5**
- The Pulpit Commentary calls v. 5 so unclear that the text may be damaged. "They come" doesn't fit the Jewish defenders and has no grammatical link to v. 4. The Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation) leaves out "they come," but the verse is still puzzling. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/33.htm
- Gill says the houses were knocked down by the Babylonian siege mounds or siege engines. He gives another reading from Jewish commentators: the defenders pulled the houses down to strengthen the wall. He sees the destruction then happening as a guarantee that the later blessings would also come true. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-33.html
- Coffman says the bodies were piled in empty houses because there was no time to bury the dead. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/33-2.html
- Geneva: the Jews thought they could beat the Babylonians but were bringing about their own ruin. God's favour causes all prosperity, and his anger causes all adversity. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Jeremiah/33.html
- Enduring Word: all the effort to defend the city would come to nothing. They should have listened to God's earlier word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-33/

**v. 6**
- Enduring Word says the promise was fulfilled partly in the return under Ezra and Nehemiah, but only truly in the new covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-33/
- Gill links "peace and truth" with the "grace and truth" that came through Christ (John 1:17). Peace is peace with God through Christ's blood. Truth is God keeping his promises, and the gospel replacing the old pictures and shadows. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-33.html
- Matthew Henry: "peace" stands for every good thing, and "truth" may mean true religion as opposed to the lies that had misled the people. God's revealed truth heals the soul (John 17:17; Psalm 107:20). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_033.cfm
- The Pulpit homiletics section calls the Lord "Jehovah-rophi" (the Lord who heals). God's treatment of sin will work. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-33.html
- Geneva: in the middle of his threats, God remembers his own people and comforts them. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Jeremiah/33.html

**v. 7**
- Gill argues that the mention of Israel (the ten northern tribes) as well as Judah shows this isn't only the return from Babylon. He reads it spiritually: God's people freed from sin, Satan and the law, and the fallen church rebuilt (Acts 15:16). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-33.html
- Enduring Word: in the new covenant, God will one day gather his scattered people from both the southern and northern kingdoms. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-33/

**v. 8**
- Enduring Word: in the new covenant, sins are not merely covered but taken away. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-33/
- The Spanish edition of Enduring Word quotes a saying that God never forgives defiled souls; he cleanses them first. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/jeremias-33/
- Gill: the cleansing is by Christ's blood (1 John 1:7; Ezekiel 36:25). The piling up of words shows how complete forgiveness is, the special blessing of the new covenant (31:34). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-33.html
- The Pulpit Commentary: restored prosperity would be worthless without spiritual cleansing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-33.html
- Geneva: there is no deliverance or joy unless we feel our sins forgiven. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Jeremiah/33.html
- Matthew Henry: sanctifying grace cleanses the filth of sin, and pardoning mercy removes its guilt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/33.htm

**v. 9**
- Geneva: a church where sins are forgiven is God's honour, so anyone who attacks it is trying to dishonour God. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Jeremiah/33.html
- Enduring Word: the people would bring honour to God's name instead of disgracing it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-33/
- Benson: the blessings would be so great that the astonished nations would fear and tremble. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/jeremiah-33.html

**vv. 10–11**
- Gill:
  - The wording echoes Psalm 106:1, and these words were sung when the second temple's foundation was laid (Ezra 3:11).
  - Bride and bridegroom stand for great joy, the reverse of 7:34.
  - He also reads it spiritually: young converts praising God's grace.
  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-33.html
- In the Spanish edition, Gill also quotes rabbis who said that in the age to come every offering will stop except the thank offering. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/geb/jeremiah-33.html
- Geneva: this was a song the Levites were appointed to sing (1 Chronicles 16:8; Psalm 136:1). https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Jeremiah/33.html
- Precept Austin quotes Feinberg: these words close the blessing used at Jewish weddings today. The word "for" explains the reason for the blessing: the Lord is good. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_33_commentary
- Guzik: the cries of a city under judgment are replaced by praise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/jeremiah/jeremiah-33.cfm
- The BibleHub chapter summary links the bridegroom to Jesus as Bridegroom (John 3:29). https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/33.htm

**vv. 12–13**
- Gill reads this "mystically": the shepherds' dwelling is God's house, where the word is preached. In v. 13, Jewish commentators (Jarchi, Kimchi, Abarbanel) take "the one who counts them" as the king. The Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase) takes it as King Messiah, and Gill agrees. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-33.html
- Geneva: the whole land of Judah will be lived in again. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Jeremiah/33.html
- Pulpit homiletics: God remembers every class of people, shepherds included. Flocks lying down means security, and counting them means there are many. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/jeremiah/33.htm

**v. 14**
- Gill: the fulfilment was five or six hundred years away. This is the best promise of all, and Gill notes that Jewish writers agree this language refers to the Messiah's times. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-33.html
- Enduring Word: the promise was fulfilled in part under Ezra and Nehemiah, and wholly in the new covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-33/
- Precept Austin: the greatest blessing is the Messiah himself being present. It calls the parallel prophecy in 23:5 not yet fulfilled. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_33_commentary

**v. 15**
- Geneva: this means the Messiah from David's house, as all the Jews testify (23:5). https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Jeremiah/33.html
- Pulpit homiletics: even if the prophet meant a line of kings, only Christ fulfils it. Israel was ruined largely by bad kings. Love isn't named here because Jeremiah's hearers needed the stress on righteousness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-33.html
- The BibleHub summary compares the Branch from Jesse in Isaiah 11:1. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/33.htm

**v. 16**
- Here the city (not the king, as in 23:6) carries the name. Commentators explain this in similar ways:
  - **Geneva:** "she" is the church, which Christ names. Christ is "our righteousness, sanctification and redemption" (1 Corinthians 1:30). https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Jeremiah/33.html
  - **Matthew Henry:** Christ gives righteousness to his church, and believers are made the righteousness of God in him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/33.htm
  - **Enduring Word:** Jerusalem carries his name because of the righteousness he imparts to her. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-33/
  - **Gill (Spanish edition):** the name Judah means one who praises the Lord. They will be saved by the Messiah from sin, Satan, the law, God's wrath and hell. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/geb/jeremiah-33.html

**v. 17**
- Gill: this can't mean David's earthly kingdom, which ended long ago (Jeconiah was recorded as childless). That kingdom was a picture of Christ's everlasting spiritual kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/geb/jeremiah-33.html
- Guzik: the claim is not that David's line reigns without a break, but that the reign never ends. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/jeremiah/jeremiah-33.cfm
- Benson: Jeremiah is foretelling the Messiah's kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/jeremiah-33.html

**v. 18 (where Protestant readings really differ)**
- **Gill (Baptist):** the Levitical priesthood has been abolished. It was a picture of Christ's priesthood, which replaces it. Gill mentions that some apply the verse to gospel ministers, but he rejects this. The New Testament never calls ministers priests or Levites. He would rather apply it to all believers as priests. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/geb/jeremiah-33.html
- **Matthew Henry (Presbyterian, my label):** takes the reading Gill rejects. Faithful ministers offering spiritual sacrifices of prayer and praise are the Levites' successors, and he cites Paul putting gospel preachers in the place of those who served at the altar (1 Corinthians 9). He also says all believers are a holy priesthood. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_033.cfm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/33.htm
- **Benson (Methodist, my label):** this is the ministry Christ set up, offering a "pure" spiritual offering in every place where a church is formed (Malachi 1:11), not only in Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/jeremiah-33.html
- **Geneva (Reformed):** this means mainly the spiritual sacrifice of thanksgiving left to the church. Christ is the everlasting priest and sacrifice that the old sacrifices pictured. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Jeremiah/33.html
- **Enduring Word (listed under Pentecostal/charismatic) and Feinberg (dispensational, my label):** Guzik quotes a commentator who says the dynasty will be permanent, served by Levitical priests who form a valid ministry. He also quotes Feinberg: this passage is especially hard for amillennialists (who don't expect a literal future reign of Christ on earth), whose only options are allegory or a "dual" way of reading. Guzik's application applies this to Israel as well as the church. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/jeremiah/jeremiah-33.cfm
- Chuck Smith explains the offerings themselves: the burnt offering stands for consecrating one's life to God, and eating the sacrifice for fellowship with him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/33-2.html
- **Critical view, as reported in the Pulpit Commentary:** some scholars say v. 18 clashes with 3:16 (the ark no longer remembered) and 31:34 (all will know the Lord). They also say a crowd of Levites and Davidic heirs is unlike Jeremiah's usual hope in one great son of David. The Pulpit Commentary itself thinks this difference in wording matters little. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/33.htm

**vv. 19–22**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the steady cycle of day and night pictures a steady supply of Davidic heirs and priests. The sand pictures their growth. Multiplying them sounds odd as a blessing, but Pulpit explains that royal relatives probably held the main state offices, and many priests were needed for worship to be done properly. The language is exaggerated, but the meaning is clear. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/33.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: the promise to the patriarchs of many descendants is applied here specifically to David's line and the priests. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/33-23.htm
- Benson: since Christ's kingdom has no end (Luke 1:32–33), this may stretch into eternity, where the saints are priests and reign with him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/jeremiah-33.html
- Gill: David has a son on his throne in Christ, who reigns for ever. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/geb/jeremiah-33.html
- Guzik quotes a writer who says God "placed the sun and the moon on the bargaining table" as a deposit to guarantee his promise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/jeremiah/jeremiah-33.cfm

**vv. 23–24 (commentators disagree on who "these people" are)**
- The Pulpit Commentary: they are unworthy people of Judah who gave up hope, not Egyptians or Babylonians as some have suggested. Calling them "this people" has a touch of contempt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/33.htm
- Benson: they are unbelieving Jews, who were in effect accusing God of breaking his promise. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/jeremiah-33.html
- Geneva: they are the Babylonians and other unbelievers. The "two families" are Judah and Israel (or Benjamin), whom God corrected only for a time. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Jeremiah/33.html
- Enduring Word: those who say God is finished with Israel as a nation commit "the great sin" of despising his people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-33/
- Precept Austin: Romans 11:28 shows ethnic Israel is still distinct from Gentiles. It favours the view that Israel will be saved at the end of history. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_33_commentary

**vv. 25–26**
- Gill: the "fixed order of heaven and earth" means the courses of the sun, moon and stars, the seasons, and seedtime and harvest. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/33-25.html
- Enduring Word: God means the physical descendants of Israel, not only spiritual ones. The new covenant reaches the whole world but doesn't set Israel aside. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-33/
- Gaebelein (quoted by Precept Austin): God's gifts and calling are not withdrawn; the covenant with David stands. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_33_commentary
- The BibleHub summary notes that the Hebrew word for "restore" (*shuv*) means to return or bring back. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/33.htm

---

### Patterns across the chapter
- **Spiritual versus literal fulfilment.** Gill, Geneva, Henry and Benson read vv. 7–26 mainly as fulfilled in Christ and the church. Enduring Word, Feinberg, Precept Austin and Gaebelein keep a future for ethnic Israel. Feinberg says plainly that this is a problem for amillennial readers. The sharpest disagreements are at vv. 18 and 24–26.
- **Prayer and material blessing.** No prosperity or word-of-faith material turned up in what I could read. Two older notes touch the theme. Matthew Henry says that where God gives righteousness and peace, he also supplies "needful" temporal wants (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/33.htm). The Pulpit homiletics section warns that God's answer may bless us in trouble rather than remove it (v. 3 above).

### Not found
Because the tool budget ran out, I have nothing on this chapter from:
- netbible.org and bibleodyssey.org (modern scholarship). The only scholarly material is what the Pulpit Commentary reports.
- The Catholic and Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org).
- The Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), Wesley's own notes, seedbed.com, ligonier.org, thegospelcoalition.org, desiringgod.org and gty.org.
- Anything on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching.
